summary: Most visitors need no visa for Grenada: CARICOM nationals move freely, and citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, most Commonwealth countries and many others are admitted without one. Nationals on Grenada's 'Port of Entry' list get a visa on arrival against a pre-clearance letter arranged before travel; everyone else needs a visitor's visa from a Grenadian mission. There is no eVisa.

notes: Canada's travel advice says it is illegal for civilians to import camouflage material or wear camouflage clothing; the UK Foreign Office says this applies to anyone, including children.
The UK Foreign Office says there are severe penalties for all drug offences; pack your luggage yourself and do not carry anything through customs for anyone else.

payments.text: Canada's travel advice says the US dollar is accepted alongside the Eastern Caribbean dollar and that ATMs are available throughout Grenada, but only at banks. No official source we could read describes card acceptance.

safety.text: Grenada is one of the calmer islands in the Caribbean and violent crime rarely involves visitors. The realistic risks are opportunistic theft from beaches and rental cars, strong currents on the Atlantic (east) coast, and hurricane season disruption.

tips.text: Canada's travel advice says hurricane season runs from early June to the end of November. The UK Foreign Office says Hurricane Beryl made landfall on Carriacou and Petite Martinique in July 2024 and that tourist infrastructure there is still reduced while rebuilding continues. Insurance covering storm disruption is worth having.

Traffic drives on the left. Canada's travel advice says you need a local driver's licence, which you can buy from a car rental agency or the central police station in St George's by showing your home licence.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Grenada?
faq.answer: Most likely not. Grenada admits citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, most Commonwealth countries and many others without a visa, and CARICOM nationals move freely. Nationals on Grenada's 'Port of Entry' list are issued a visa on arrival, but only with a pre-clearance letter obtained through a Grenadian mission first. Everyone else needs a visitor's visa from a Grenadian mission before flying; there is no eVisa.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Grenada without a visa?
faq.answer: The immigration officer writes the period on your entry stamp. Grenada's official list states it only for some nationalities (30 days for Argentina and China, 60 for Cuba, 90 for Brazil); the UK, US and Canadian governments say 3 months (90 days) for their citizens, and CARICOM nationals get a definite entry of six months. Extensions are handled by the Immigration Department in St George's and should be applied for before your stamp expires.

faq.question: Is there an arrival form for Grenada?
faq.answer: No official source we could read describes Grenada's arrival form or says whether it can be completed online. The UK Foreign Office says you must declare anything that may be prohibited or subject to tax or duty, so follow the instructions given on your flight.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate for Grenada?
faq.answer: Only if you are aged one or over and arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, or spent more than 12 hours in transit at an airport in one. WHO's risk countries are in tropical Africa and South and Central America, and include Trinidad.

faq.question: Can I drive in Grenada on my own license?
faq.answer: Not on its own. Canada's travel advice says you need a local driver's licence, which you can buy from a car rental agency or the central police station in St George's by showing your valid home licence. Traffic drives on the left.

faq.question: Does CARICOM free movement apply in Grenada?
faq.answer: Yes. Grenada is a member of CARICOM and the OECS, so nationals of member states are granted a definite entry of up to six months on arrival, without a visa and generally without needing to show onward tickets in the way other visitors do.
